strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing real challenges in fine-grained MoE training with clear quantitative evidence (Equation 4, Figure 3, Table 1)
Technically sound memory-efficient backward pass algorithm achieving minimum activation memory (O(2Td + 4TKn)) matching dense models, with clever dS computation avoiding Y and dY caching
Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation with extensive kernel-level profiling, multiple strong baselines, thorough ablation studies (Section E), and fair comparisons
Meaningful practical speedups (45% memory reduction, 1.86x forward/backward throughput on H100) with end-to-end validation (213B tokens/day on 64 H100s)
Novel contributions in gathering fusion for backward K-dimension GEMM and application of Ping-Pong scheduling to address MoE's heavy epilogues
Reproducibility and accessibility through open-source implementation in CuTe-DSL, detailed algorithms, extensive configuration tables, and ablation studies
Token rounding routing provides simple yet effective solution to tile quantization with bounded deviation guarantee and empirical quality preservation (16% speedup in sparse settings)
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: primarily co-designs existing techniques (gather fusion, Ping-Pong scheduling, dS optimization) rather than introducing fundamental innovations; similar ideas acknowledged in prior work (ScatterMoE, MoMoE, Flash Attention 3, Megatron)

GPU-specific optimizations with limited portability: heavily tailored to Hopper/Blackwell architectures (TMA, WGMMA, Tensor Memory); Blackwell gather fusion requires workarounds (relay mechanism); unclear generalization to other vendors or older architectures
Incremental improvements over existing work: ~40% speedup over ScatterMoE is substantial but not transformative; some configurations show modest improvements (e.g., 7B backward: 8.3% over ScatterMoE)

Token rounding evaluation limited to small models (0.5B/1.4B for full train-eval); inference uses standard TC routing (not TR), limiting practical benefit to training phase; performance degrades when T̄_e/M_tile = 1; method is microbatch-level with unclear interaction with dynamic shapes

Experimental scope: end-to-end training mostly on 7B models; largest model (DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp, 685B) only kernel-level benchmarking; limited Blackwell results; would benefit from larger-scale end-to-end training validation

Dense presentation with scattered technical details obscuring main insights; 17-page main paper plus extensive appendix; multiple design choices (Figure 9 strategies, rounding subroutines) lack unified justification
Activation memory claim is slightly weakened: temporary Y variable still materialized (footnote 8), though transient allocation strategy mitigates this
Missing comparisons with recent methods like TMA-adaptive FP8 Grouped GEMM; limited discussion of distributed training with expert parallelism or alternative approaches

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing real challenges in modern fine-grained and sparse MoE training
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple baselines, GPU generations, and model scales with detailed kernel-level profiling
Concrete and significant practical improvements: 45% memory reduction, 1.86x throughput speedup, demonstrated large-scale training
Solid engineering with multiple well-integrated optimization techniques (gather fusion, epilogue fusion, async IO overlapping)
Thorough ablation studies and extensive appendices demonstrating technical competence
Open-source commitment to release kernels, providing value to the community
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: gather fusion, epilogue fusion, and ping-pong scheduling are known techniques; contribution is primarily engineering-driven combination and GPU specialization
Hardware-specific design tightly coupled to Hopper/Blackwell; generalizability to other accelerators unclear and limited broader impact
Fairness of baseline comparisons: ScatterMoE/MoMoE in Triton have inherent optimization limitations; DeepGEMM requires custom kernels for complete comparison
Token rounding evaluation incomplete: downstream task evaluation limited to 1.4B parameters only; improvements modest except in extreme sparsity (K/E ≤ 1/64); no full training runs on larger models
End-to-end evaluation limited: most results at layer/kernel level; full training throughput uses non-standard lm-engine codebase; no inference performance reported
Methodological concerns: memory comparison somewhat circular (SonicMoE by design materializes less); upper bounds exclude router computation; token rounding as 'drop-in replacement' overstated
Incomplete exploration of design sensitivity: limited ablation on tile sizes and warpgroup configurations; arbitrary-seeming parameter choices
Code unavailable at review time; reproducibility gaps in specific architectural choices and lm-engine integration
